content: A natural reservoir, also known as a nidus, refers to the long-term host of a pathogen responsible for an infectious disease. In many cases, these hosts do not exhibit symptoms of the disease carried by the pathogen, or the disease remains asymptomatic and non-lethal in them. Identifying natural reservoirs is crucial as it helps to elucidate the complete life cycle of infectious diseases, thereby enabling effective prevention and control strategies. Examples of natural reservoirs include the following: Field mice serve as reservoirs for hantaviruses and Lassa fever. Marmots, black rats, prairie dogs, chipmunks, and squirrels are reservoirs for the bubonic plague. Armadillos and opossums act as reservoirs for Chagas disease. Ticks are reservoirs for diseases such as babesiosis and Rocky Mountain spotted fever. Ground squirrels, porcupines, and chipmunks are reservoirs for Colorado tick fever. Mosquitoes serve as reservoirs for filariasis and malaria. Snails are reservoirs for schistosomiasis and swimmer's itch. Pigs act as reservoirs for cestode worm infections. Raccoons, skunks, foxes, and bats are reservoirs for rabies. Shellfish can act as reservoirs for cholera. Fowl, such as ducks and geese, are reservoirs for avian influenza. Some diseases, however, lack non-human reservoirs. Notable examples include poliomyelitis and smallpox, which are exclusively human diseases. The concept of a natural reservoir can also be extended to asymptomatic human carriers of infectious agents. A well-known example of this is the case of Typhoid Mary, who was an asymptomatic carrier of the bacterium causing typhoid fever. For certain diseases, the natural reservoir remains unidentified. This is the case with Ebola virus disease, where the natural host of the virus has yet to be determined.
